image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA-H-8083-32B, Dry Sump Lubrication System Operation

notes.front: A mechanic traces oil in a piston dry-sump system after it has lubricated the bearings and drained to the sumps. What is the next component?
notes.choices:
A) The scavenger pump, which sends it through the cooler to the tank
B) The full-flow filter
C) The pressure pump
D) The suction screen on the tank line
notes.back: A) The scavenger pump, which sends it through the cooler to the tank
notes.choicesExplained: C: that draws from the tank, not the sumps. B: it sits after the pressure pump. D: that is on the pressure pump inlet.
notes.explanation: Scavenger pumps pick up sump oil; on dry-sump engines it passes through the cooler and back to the tank.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Dry Sump Lubrication System Operation”, PDF page 259
notes.evidence: Oil collected in these sumps is picked up by gear or gerotor-type scavenger pumps as quickly as it accumulates.

notes.front: After refitting and filling an oil tank, what should follow?
notes.back: Run the engine at least two minutes, then check the level and top up to the dipstick mark.
notes.explanation: The run fills the system, lowering the tank level.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Lubrication System Maintenance Practices”, PDF page 260
notes.evidence: After the oil tank has been filled, the engine should be run for at least two minutes. Then, the oil level should be checked and, if necessary, sufficient oil should be added to bring the oil up to the proper level on the dipstick.

notes.front: High oil temperature points to an obstructed oil cooler. What is the remedy in the troubleshooting table?
notes.back: Check the cooler for blocked or deformed passages; replace it if defective.
notes.explanation: Obstruction in cooler passages is listed as a cause of high or low oil temperature.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Troubleshooting Oil Systems (Figure 6-30)”, PDF page 265
notes.evidence: Check cooler for blocked or deformed passages.

notes.front: What must be done with pressure and scavenge oil screens?
notes.back: Remove, inspect and clean them at the manufacturer's intervals, as sludge collects on them.
notes.explanation: Metal particles found may point to internal wear, damage or even failure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Pressure & Scavenge Oil Screens”, PDF page 261
notes.evidence: Sludge accumulates on the pressure and scavenges oil screens during engine operation. [Figure 6-26] These screens must be removed, inspected, and cleaned at the intervals specified

notes.front: Why must the container catching oil from a screen housing be clean?
notes.back: Contamination already in it would give a false indication of engine condition, perhaps causing premature engine removal.
notes.explanation: The collected oil is examined for foreign particles.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Pressure & Scavenge Oil Screens”, PDF page 261
notes.evidence: Any contamination already present in the container gives a false indication of the engine condition. This could result in a premature engine removal.

notes.front: A mechanic drains a screen housing into a used drip tray, finds metal flakes, and recommends engine removal. What was the error?
notes.choices:
A) The screen should have been reinstalled uncleaned
B) Screens should never be removed between overhauls
C) Metal particles are always normal
D) The container was not clean, so the flakes may not have come from the engine
notes.back: D) The container was not clean, so the flakes may not have come from the engine
notes.choicesExplained: B: they are removed and cleaned at set intervals. C: they may indicate wear, damage or failure. A: it must be cleaned before reinstalling.
notes.explanation: Prior contamination gives a false indication and could cause premature removal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Pressure & Scavenge Oil Screens”, PDF page 261
notes.evidence: The container must be clean so that the oil collected in it can be examined for foreign particles.

notes.front: What are two of the main contaminants of oil in service?
notes.back: Any two: gasoline, moisture, acids, dirt, carbon, metallic particles.
notes.explanation: Their build-up is why the whole system is drained and refilled at regular intervals.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Recommendations for Changing Oil”, PDF page 263
notes.evidence: Because of the accumulation of these harmful substances, common practice is to drain the entire lubrication system at regular intervals and refill with new oil.

notes.front: An owner asks why oil is changed on a schedule when the level has not dropped. What is the best answer?
notes.choices:
A) Oil always evaporates at a fixed rate
B) The filter cannot be changed without draining
C) Harmful substances such as moisture, acids and metal build up in service oil
D) New oil has a higher SAE number
notes.back: C) Harmful substances such as moisture, acids and metal build up in service oil
notes.choicesExplained: A: the reason given is accumulating contaminants. B: filters are changed on their own schedule too. D: the grade stays the same.
notes.explanation: Accumulating contaminants reduce the oil's ability to protect moving parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Recommendations for Changing Oil”, PDF page 263
notes.evidence: Oil, in service, is constantly exposed to many harmful substances that reduce its ability to protect moving parts.

notes.front: In the handbook's example, what is a typical oil change interval for engines with a pressure screen system?
notes.back: 25 hours, with pressure screen cleaning and a sump suction screen check.
notes.explanation: Full-flow filter engines typically change at 50 hours.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil & Filter Change & Screen Cleaning”, PDF page 263
notes.evidence: A typical interval for oil change is 25 hours, along with a pressure screen cleaning and oil sump suction screen check for all engines employing a pressure screen system.

notes.front: In the handbook's example, what do typical 50-hour oil changes include for full-flow filter engines?
notes.back: Oil filter replacement and a suction screen check.
notes.explanation: A maximum of 4 months between services is also recommended.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil & Filter Change & Screen Cleaning”, PDF page 263
notes.evidence: Typical 50-hour interval oil changes generally include the oil filter replacement and suction screen check for all engines using full-flow filtration systems.

notes.front: A full-flow-filter piston engine flew 20 hours in the 4 months since its last oil service. Under the manufacturer example, is service due?
notes.choices:
A) No, not until 50 hours
B) Yes: 4 months is the maximum time between services
C) No, not until 25 hours
D) Only if the oil looks dark
notes.back: B) Yes: 4 months is the maximum time between services
notes.choicesExplained: A: the 4-month limit applies as well. C: that interval is for pressure screen systems. D: the example sets a calendar maximum.
notes.explanation: The example sets both hour intervals and a 4-month maximum.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil & Filter Change & Screen Cleaning”, PDF page 263
notes.evidence: A time maximum of 4 months between servicing is also recommended for oil system service.

notes.front: How are ferrous and nonferrous particles checked in a cut-open spin-on filter?
notes.back: A clean magnet finds ferrous particles; pouring the solvent through a clean filter or towel under bright light shows nonferrous ones.
notes.explanation: The can is cut open with a special cutter to remove the element.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil Filter/Screen Content Inspection”, PDF page 264
notes.evidence: Use a clean magnet and check for any ferrous metal particles in the filter or varsol solution. Then, take the remaining varsol and pour it through a clean filter or shop towel. Using a bright light, inspect for any nonferrous metals.

notes.front: What do metal particles, shavings or flakes in the oil filter or screens indicate?
notes.back: Premature or excessive engine component wear.
notes.explanation: Abnormal metal content may need further service to find the source.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil Filter/Screen Content Inspection”, PDF page 263
notes.evidence: Check for premature or excessive engine component wear that is indicated by the presence of metal particles, shavings, or flakes in the oil filter element or screens.

notes.front: A cut-open filter element shows shiny flakes that a clean magnet does not pick up. What does this suggest?
notes.choices:
A) Nonferrous metal, pointing to wear of non-steel parts
B) No wear, since the magnet found nothing
C) Ferrous wear from steel parts
D) Normal carbon deposits
notes.back: A) Nonferrous metal, pointing to wear of non-steel parts
notes.choicesExplained: B: the magnet only finds ferrous metal. C: those would stick to the magnet. D: shiny flakes are metal, which indicates wear.
notes.explanation: The magnet checks ferrous metal; a bright light shows nonferrous metals.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil Filter/Screen Content Inspection”, PDF page 264
notes.evidence: Using a bright light, inspect for any nonferrous metals.

notes.front: How is a spin-on oil filter installed?
notes.back: Coat the rubber gasket with engine oil, fit the filter, then torque and safety it.
notes.explanation: Spin-on filters generally carry their own installation instructions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Assembly of & Installation of Oil Filters”, PDF page 264
notes.evidence: Place a coating of engine oil on the rubber gasket, install the filter, torque and safety it.

notes.front: What are two causes of excessive oil consumption in the troubleshooting table?
notes.back: Any two: oil line leakage, accessory seal leakage, low grade of oil, failing or failed bearing.
notes.explanation: Each has its own isolation check, such as looking for leaks after engine operation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Troubleshooting Oil Systems (Figure 6-30)”, PDF page 265
notes.evidence: Excessive oil consumption Oil line leakage. Check external lines for evidence of oil leakage. Replace or repair defective lines. Accessory seal leakage.

notes.front: A newly overhauled engine run on AD oil from the start burns oil heavily. Which cause does the handbook point to?
notes.choices:
A) AD additives retarding break-in of the rings and cylinder walls
B) A blocked tank vent
C) An open filter bypass valve
D) A low viscosity index
notes.back: A) AD additives retarding break-in of the rings and cylinder walls
notes.choicesExplained: D: nothing in the case points to viscosity. B: that is not a listed consumption cause. C: that affects filtering, not consumption.
notes.explanation: The handbook warns AD oil in a new or overhauled engine may cause high consumption.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Requirements & Characteristics of Reciprocating Engine Lubricants”, PDF page 250
notes.evidence: If ashless dispersant oil is used in a new engine, or a newly overhauled engine, high oil consumption might possibly be experienced.

notes.front: What are two causes of high or low indicated oil pressure in the troubleshooting table?
notes.back: Any two: defective gauge, inadequate supply, diluted oil, clogged screen, wrong viscosity, relief valve misadjusted.
notes.explanation: Each is isolated and remedied separately, for example by checking relief valve adjustment.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Troubleshooting Oil Systems (Figure 6-30)”, PDF page 265
notes.evidence: Oil viscosity incorrect. Make sure correct oil is being used. Drain engine and tank; refill tank. Oil pump pressure relief valve adjustment incorrect. Check pressure relief valve adjustment.

notes.front: What are two causes of high or low indicated oil temperature in the troubleshooting table?
notes.back: Any two: defective gauge, inadequate supply, diluted oil, tank obstruction, clogged screen, cooler obstruction.
notes.explanation: Oil level too high in the tank is also listed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Troubleshooting Oil Systems (Figure 6-30)”, PDF page 265
notes.evidence: High or low indicated oil temperature Defective temperature gauge. Check indicator. Replace indicator if defective. Inadequate oil supply. Check oil quantity. Fill oil tank.

notes.front: An engine's oil pressure is low, the gauge checks good, quantity is correct, and the screen is clean. Which listed item should be checked next?
notes.choices:
A) The chip detector wiring
B) The ignition timing
C) The oil cooler air-exit flap
D) The oil type and viscosity, and the relief valve adjustment
notes.back: D) The oil type and viscosity, and the relief valve adjustment
notes.choicesExplained: B: it is not on the oil pressure list. C: it controls temperature, not pressure. A: it is not a pressure cause.
notes.explanation: Wrong viscosity oil and incorrect relief valve adjustment remain on the table's pressure list.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Troubleshooting Oil Systems (Figure 6-30)”, PDF page 265
notes.evidence: Oil viscosity incorrect. Make sure correct oil is being used. Drain engine and tank; refill tank. Oil pump pressure relief valve adjustment incorrect. Check pressure relief valve adjustment.

notes.front: Why do turbine engines use a less viscous lubricant than piston engines?
notes.back: They lack reciprocating motion and use ball and roller (antifriction) bearings.
notes.explanation: The oil must still carry load well while flowing easily.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Requirements for Turbine Engine Lubricants”, PDF page 264
notes.evidence: Due to the absence of reciprocating motion and the presence of ball and roller bearings (antifriction bearings), the turbine engine uses a less viscous lubricant.

notes.front: What advantage does synthetic turbine oil have over petroleum oil in deposits?
notes.back: A lower tendency to deposit lacquer and coke, because it does not evaporate solvents at high temperature.
notes.explanation: Synthetic oils were developed to meet turbine oil's many requirements.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Requirements for Turbine Engine Lubricants”, PDF page 264
notes.evidence: It has a lower tendency to deposit lacquer and coke (solids left after solvents have been evaporated) because it does not evaporate the solvents from the oil at high temperature.

notes.front: A mechanic servicing a turbine engine is offered aviation piston grade 100 oil because "it is thicker and protects better". What is wrong?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: thicker oil is always better
B) Grade 100 is too thin for turbines
C) Any oil works if the filter is changed
D) Turbine engines need a less viscous synthetic oil approved for them
notes.back: D) Turbine engines need a less viscous synthetic oil approved for them
notes.choicesExplained: A: turbine oil must flow well and have low volatility. B: it is thicker, and turbines use a less viscous oil. C: the oil type must suit the engine.
notes.explanation: Turbines lack reciprocating motion and use antifriction bearings, so they use a less viscous lubricant met by synthetic oils.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Requirements for Turbine Engine Lubricants”, PDF page 264
notes.evidence: The many requirements for lubricating oils are met in the synthetic oils developed specifically for turbine engines.

notes.front: Where can turbine oil exposure limits generally be found?
notes.back: In the material safety data sheets.
notes.explanation: Prolonged breathing of vapour above limits may cause lightheadedness, dizziness and nausea.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Oil Health & Safety Precautions”, PDF page 265
notes.evidence: Information on established limits on exposure to turbine oil can generally be found in the material safety data sheets (MSDS).

notes.front: Why must petroleum products never be siphoned by mouth?
notes.back: Because of the risk of ingestion.
notes.explanation: If turbine oil is swallowed, call a doctor at once and identify the product and amount.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Oil Health & Safety Precautions”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: Because of the risk of ingestion, petroleum products should never be siphoned by mouth.

notes.front: What does prolonged skin contact with turbine oil cause, and what is the remedy?
notes.back: Irritation and dermatitis; wash thoroughly with soap and warm water and remove soaked clothing.
notes.explanation: Protective clothing, gloves and eye protection should be used when handling it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Oil Health & Safety Precautions”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: Prolonged or repeated contact of turbine oil with the skin can cause irritation and dermatitis. In case of skin contact, wash the skin thoroughly with soap and warm water.

notes.front: Turbine oil splashes into a mechanic's eye while servicing. What should be done?
notes.choices:
A) Wipe it with a petroleum solvent
B) Carry on and wash at the end of the shift
C) Siphon the remaining oil by mouth to finish quickly
D) Flush the eye with fresh water until the irritation subsides
notes.back: D) Flush the eye with fresh water until the irritation subsides
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is for painted surfaces. B: the handbook calls for flushing. C: petroleum products are never siphoned by mouth.
notes.explanation: The handbook's precaution for eye contact is flushing with fresh water.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Oil Health & Safety Precautions”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: If turbine oil contacts the eyes, flush the eyes with fresh water until the irritation subsides.

notes.front: What does the spectrometric oil analysis program measure?
notes.back: Minute metallic elements (wear metals and additives) in an oil sample, in parts per million by weight.
notes.explanation: Every oil in service carries microscopic wear metals picked up as it circulates.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Spectrometric Oil Analysis Program”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: Oil analysis programs identify and measure these particles in parts per million (PPM) by weight.

notes.front: What does a rise in parts per million of certain metals indicate?
notes.back: Possible component wear or impending engine failure.
notes.explanation: If wear metals rise beyond a normal rate, the operator can be told quickly so repair or inspection is ordered.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Spectrometric Oil Analysis Program”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: An increase in PPM of certain materials can be a sign of component wear or impending failure of the engine.

notes.front: Three successive oil samples show copper rising faster than the normal rate. What should happen?
notes.choices:
A) Change to a higher grade of oil
B) Nothing until a chip light comes on
C) Notify the operator promptly so repair or a specific inspection can be ordered
D) Discard the samples as contaminated
notes.back: C) Notify the operator promptly so repair or a specific inspection can be ordered
notes.choicesExplained: B: analysis aims to catch problems before failure. A: the grade does not address wear. D: a rising trend is the warning sign.
notes.explanation: Rising wear metals beyond the normal rate are the trigger for prompt action.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Spectrometric Oil Analysis Program”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: If the amount of wear metals increases beyond a normal rate, then the operator can be notified quickly so repair or a recommendation of a specific maintenance procedure or inspection can be ordered.

notes.front: In oil analysis, which parts does iron wear indicate?
notes.back: Rings, shafts, gears, valve train, cylinder walls and, in some engines, pistons.
notes.explanation: Identifying the metal helps identify which components are wearing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Typical Wear Metals & Additives”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: Iron—wear from rings, shafts, gears, valve train, cylinder walls, and pistons in some engines.

notes.front: In oil analysis, which parts does aluminium indicate?
notes.back: Pistons, rod bearings and certain bushings.
notes.explanation: Each wear metal is linked to its likely engine source.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Typical Wear Metals & Additives”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: Aluminum—indicates wear of pistons, rod bearings, and certain types of bushings.

notes.front: Which is the most critical lubricating point in a gas turbine engine?
notes.back: The exhaust turbine bearing, because of the high temperature there.
notes.explanation: Some engines add bleed-air cooling to the oil cooling of that bearing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Engine Lubrication Systems”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: The exhaust turbine bearing is the most critical lubricating point in a gas turbine engine because of the high temperature normally present.

notes.front: Besides the pressure relief system, what other two turbine oil system classes does the handbook name?
notes.back: The full flow type, whose pressure varies with engine speed, and the total loss type for short-duration engines.
notes.explanation: The pressure relief system is the most widely used; full flow is mostly on large fan engines.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Engine Lubrication Systems”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: the full flow type of system, in which the pressure varies with engine speed, and the total loss system, used in engines that are for short duration operation (target drones, missiles, etc.).

notes.front: Why does turbine bearing lubrication normally need an oil cooler?
notes.back: Cooling is a major function of the oil in turbine engines.
notes.explanation: The coolers are air-cooled and/or fuel-cooled, and the fuel-cooled type also heats the fuel against ice.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Engine Lubrication Systems”, PDF page 267
notes.evidence: Since cooling is a major function of the oil in turbine engines, the lubricating oil for bearing cooling normally requires an oil cooler.

notes.front: A short-life target drone engine has no oil return: oil is used once and lost. Which system class is this?
notes.choices:
A) Total loss
B) Full flow
C) Wet sump
D) Pressure relief
notes.back: A) Total loss
notes.choicesExplained: D: that keeps a somewhat constant pressure and recirculates oil. B: its pressure varies with speed but oil still recirculates. C: that describes where oil is stored, and it recirculates.
notes.explanation: The total loss system is for short-duration engines such as target drones and missiles.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Engine Lubrication Systems”, PDF page 266
notes.evidence: the total loss system, used in engines that are for short duration operation (target drones, missiles, etc.).

notes.front: Why are oil filters particularly important in gas turbines?
notes.back: High-speed ball and roller bearings are damaged quickly by contaminated oil, and small oil passages clog easily.
notes.explanation: Filters remove foreign particles before oil reaches those parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Oil Filters”, PDF page 269
notes.evidence: This is particularly important in gas turbines as very high engine speeds are attained; the antifriction types of ball and roller bearings would become damaged quite rapidly if lubricated with contaminated oil.

notes.front: What does the antidrain check valve in a turbine oil filter assembly do, and what opens it?
notes.back: Stops tank oil draining into the engine sumps when stopped; it needs 4 to 6 psi to open.
notes.explanation: It is normally spring loaded closed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Oil Filters”, PDF page 270
notes.evidence: An antidrain check valve is incorporated into the assembly to prevent the oil in the tank from draining down into the engine sumps when the engine is not operating. This check valve is normally spring loaded closed with 4 to 6 psi needed to open it.

notes.front: What are last-chance filters?
notes.back: Fine-mesh screens at each bearing that strain oil just before the spray nozzles.
notes.explanation: They catch contaminants that could plug a nozzle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Oil Filters”, PDF page 270
notes.evidence: there are fine-mesh screens called last chance filters for straining the oil just before it passes from the spray nozzles onto the bearing surfaces.

notes.front: On a walk-round, a mechanic sees the mechanical pop-out on a turbine oil filter extended. What does it mean?
notes.choices:
A) The oil is too cold to read quantity
B) The chip detector has caught metal
C) The filter has been in bypass, so unfiltered oil has reached the bearings
D) The tank is overfull
notes.back: C) The filter has been in bypass, so unfiltered oil has reached the bearings
notes.choicesExplained: A: the indicator shows bypass, not temperature. B: that is a separate device. D: that is read on the sight gauge or dipstick.
notes.explanation: The pop-out marks bypass mode; filtering was lost, though bearings kept getting oil.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Oil Filters”, PDF page 270
notes.evidence: If this occurs, the filtering action is lost, allowing unfiltered oil to be pumped to the bearings. However, this prevents the bearings from receiving no oil at all.

notes.front: Must fuel always pass through a fuel-oil cooler, and must the oil?
notes.back: Fuel must; oil may bypass through a thermostatic valve if no cooling is needed.
notes.explanation: The thermostatic valve controls oil flow through the exchanger.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Fuel-Oil Coolers”, PDF page 273
notes.evidence: Fuel flowing to the engine must pass through the heat exchanger; however, there is a thermostatic valve that controls the oil flow, and the oil may bypass the cooler if no cooling is needed.

notes.front: On a cold-soaked climb, a turbine's fuel temperature must be kept up to prevent icing. Which component helps?
notes.choices:
A) The deoiler
B) The air-oil cooler
C) The fuel-oil cooler, where hot oil heats the fuel
D) The magnetic chip detector
notes.back: C) The fuel-oil cooler, where hot oil heats the fuel
notes.choicesExplained: A: it separates oil from breather air. B: it rejects heat to air, not fuel. D: it catches ferrous particles.
notes.explanation: In the fuel-oil cooler the fuel cools the oil and the oil heats the fuel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Engine Lubrication Systems”, PDF page 267
notes.evidence: To ensure proper temperature, oil is routed through either air-cooled and/or fuel-cooled oil coolers. This system is used to also heat (regulate) the fuel to prevent ice in the fuel.

notes.front: Where are magnetic chip detectors generally located?
notes.back: In the scavenge lines for each scavenge pump, the oil tank and the oil sumps.
notes.explanation: Scavenge oil flows past them, so particles stick to the magnet.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Magnetic Chip Detectors”, PDF page 274
notes.evidence: Chip detectors are placed in several locations but generally are in the scavenge lines for each scavenge pump, oil tank, and in the oil sumps.

notes.front: During maintenance a chip detector shows no metal. What is done with it?
notes.back: It is cleaned, refitted and safety wired.
notes.explanation: If metal is found, the source must be investigated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Magnetic Chip Detectors”, PDF page 274
notes.evidence: During maintenance, the chip detectors are removed from the engine and inspected for metal; if none is found, the detector is cleaned, replaced, and safety wired.

notes.front: At a scheduled inspection, a turbine's scavenge-line chip detector carries a fuzz of steel particles. What next?
notes.choices:
A) Clean it, refit and safety wire it, with no further action
B) Change the oil grade
C) Investigate to find the source of the metal
D) Remove the detector permanently
notes.back: C) Investigate to find the source of the metal
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is only when no metal is found. B: grade does not explain metal. D: it is part of the oil system monitoring.
notes.explanation: Metal on a chip detector calls for an investigation of its source.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Magnetic Chip Detectors”, PDF page 274
notes.evidence: If metal is found on a chip detector, an investigation should be made to find the source of the metal

notes.front: What does the breather pressurising system do?
notes.back: Ensures a proper spray pattern from the main bearing jets and gives the scavenge system a pressure head.
notes.explanation: It gathers bearing compartment and tank vapour to the deoiler, which vents the air.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Breather Pressurizing System”, PDF page 275
notes.evidence: The breather pressurizing system ensures a proper oil spray pattern from the main bearing oil jets and furnishes a pressure head to the scavenge system.

notes.front: When must turbine engine oil be checked?
notes.back: Just after shutdown.
notes.explanation: Oil is checked with a dipstick or sight gauge against its level markings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Engine Oil System Maintenance”, PDF page 277
notes.evidence: In general, aircraft engine oil is checked with a dipstick or a sight gauge. There are markings on the stick or around the sight gauge to determine the correct level. Turbine engines must be checked just after shutdown.

notes.front: How often should a turbine engine's oil filter be removed?
notes.back: At every regular inspection, then disassembled, cleaned, and worn elements replaced.
notes.explanation: Intervals for oil changes vary widely between models, so the manufacturer's instructions govern.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Engine Oil System Maintenance”, PDF page 277
notes.evidence: The oil filter should be removed at every regular inspection. It should be disassembled, cleaned, and any worn or damaged filter elements replaced.

notes.front: A turbine aircraft landed three hours ago, and the mechanic now checks oil quantity. What does the handbook say?
notes.choices:
A) Check only before the first flight of the day
B) Three hours later is ideal for settling
C) Turbine oil should be checked just after shutdown
D) Check only at the next filter change
notes.back: C) Turbine oil should be checked just after shutdown
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook says just after shutdown. A: the handbook gives just after shutdown. D: servicing oil is a routine function.
notes.explanation: The handbook states turbine engines must be checked just after shutdown.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Turbine Engine Oil System Maintenance”, PDF page 277
notes.evidence: Turbine engines must be checked just after shutdown.

notes.front: In a turbine system, what may be done if the air temperature is abnormally low?
notes.back: Change to a lighter grade of oil; some engines allow an immersion-type oil heater.
notes.explanation: The oil choice follows the climatic conditions of operation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil Tank (turbine)”, PDF page 268
notes.evidence: If the air temperature is abnormally low, the oil may be changed to a lighter grade. Some engines may provide for the installation of an immersion-type oil heater.

notes.front: Below what temperature is preheating of a piston engine and its oil tank normally required?
notes.back: Below 20 °F, whatever oil is used.
notes.explanation: Even ashless dispersant grades need preheat below that temperature.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Requirements & Characteristics of Reciprocating Engine Lubricants”, PDF page 249
notes.evidence: At temperatures below 20 °F, preheating of the engine and oil supply tank is normally required regardless of the type of oil used.

notes.front: A piston aircraft on AD multigrade oil must depart at 10 °F. What does the handbook say?
notes.choices:
A) No preheat is needed with AD oil
B) Switch to straight mineral oil instead
C) Dilute the oil with jet fuel
D) Preheat the engine and oil tank, as is normally required below 20 °F
notes.back: D) Preheat the engine and oil tank, as is normally required below 20 °F
notes.choicesExplained: A: preheat is required regardless of oil type. B: that does not remove the need for preheat. C: oil dilution uses gasoline in reciprocating engines, and preheat is the stated need.
notes.explanation: Below 20 °F the handbook requires preheating regardless of the oil used.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Requirements & Characteristics of Reciprocating Engine Lubricants”, PDF page 249
notes.evidence: At temperatures below 20 °F, preheating of the engine and oil supply tank is normally required regardless of the type of oil used.

notes.front: An engine-driven oil pump's gears seize during a ground run, yet the accessory gearbox is undamaged. Which feature protected it?
notes.choices:
A) The oil filter bypass valve
B) The regulating (relief) valve
C) The pump shaft shear section
D) The antidrain check valve
notes.back: C) The pump shaft shear section
notes.choicesExplained: A: it routes oil round a clogged filter. B: it limits output pressure, not seized-gear torque. D: it stops tank oil draining into the sumps.
notes.explanation: The shear section makes the shaft shear if the pump gears seize and stop turning.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil Pump (turbine)”, PDF page 269
notes.evidence: Also shown is the shaft shear section that causes the shaft to shear if the pump gears should seize up and not turn.

notes.front: On a very cold start, the oil cooler core is packed with congealed oil. How does oil still get through the cooler?
notes.choices:
A) It cannot, so the engine is starved
B) Through the air tubes
C) Through the core under higher pressure
D) Round the bypass jacket to the outlet, without passing through the core
notes.back: D) Round the bypass jacket to the outlet, without passing through the core
notes.choicesExplained: B: air, not oil, passes through the tubes. C: congealed oil blocks the core. A: the bypass jacket gives a route round the core.
notes.explanation: Oil takes the bypass route when cold or when the core is blocked with congealed oil.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil Cooler”, PDF page 255
notes.evidence: The oil can also pass from the inlet completely around the bypass jacket to the outlet without passing through the core. Oil follows this bypass route when the oil is cold or when the core is blocked with thick, congealed oil.

notes.front: How does straight mineral oil differ from ashless dispersant oil in use?
notes.back: Mineral: no additives but a pour depressant and antioxidant, used for break-in. AD: dispersant additives, for normal service after break-in.
notes.explanation: AD additives may retard ring break-in, while mineral oil lacks dispersant additives.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Requirements & Characteristics of Reciprocating Engine Lubricants”, PDF page 250
notes.evidence: This condition can be avoided by the use of mineral oil until normal oil consumption is obtained, then change to the ashless dispersant oil.

notes.front: What is the difference between a W after an SAE number, as in 20W, and a W in front of the grade number?
notes.back: After: suitable for winter use. Before: the oil is ashless dispersant.
notes.explanation: The handbook warns the two must not be confused.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Requirements & Characteristics of Reciprocating Engine Lubricants”, PDF page 248
notes.evidence: This should not be confused with the W used in front of the grade or weight number that indicates the oil is of the ashless dispersant type.

notes.front: In turbine systems, how does a regulating valve differ from a true relief valve?
notes.back: A regulating valve keeps pressure within limits all the time; a relief valve opens only above the maximum.
notes.explanation: Regulated systems keep pressure fairly constant; variable-pressure systems let it vary with rpm.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Oil Pressure Regulating Valve (turbine)”, PDF page 270
notes.evidence: It is more of a regulating valve than a relief valve because it keeps the pressure in the system within certain limits other than only opening when the absolute maximum pressure of the system is exceeded.

notes.front: How does a fuel-oil cooler differ from an air-oil cooler?
notes.back: The fuel-oil cooler uses fuel as coolant and heats the fuel; the air-oil cooler rejects heat to air.
notes.explanation: Many turbine engines use both types.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B, 2023), “Air-Oil Coolers”, PDF page 273
notes.evidence: This cooler may be air-cooled or fuel-cooled and many engines use both.
